title: New approaches to education in New Zealand
titleCn: 新西兰教育新方法：学校改革实验

paragraphs.text: You will hear part of a lecture about education in New Zealand.
First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
Morning, everyone. The question I'm going to address today is this:
What's the best way to educate children in the twenty-first century? Because some schools here in New Zealand are experimenting with new approaches to education.

So first, what's the background to the debate? Well, one leading academic in this field is Dr. Paul Stanley. He believes that traditional schools emphasize the wrong things. At the moment, schools don't focus enough on the emotional or creative needs of children. Instead, it's all about working to obtain a qualification, which is a mistake in his view, and this is an idea that's supported by a number of educationalists.
In two thousand and nine, Dr. Stanley produced a report, and I recommend that you study it carefully.
Among a number of important conclusions is one about the way schools are managed.

He argues that day-to-day school timetables, the teaching syllabus and so on, are over-regulated by the government when in fact these things should be organized locally at a community level because every school is different.
Turning now to international studies, the situation seems to be broadly similar in Australia, the United States, and the Netherlands.
A new type of school, researchers argue, would have advantages, not for all children perhaps, but the boys especially would benefit because they're the ones who fail most often in current schools.
Another interesting suggestion comes from Robert Finley, an anthropologist.

Finley's research has found that if there are more than, say, a hundred and fifty students in a school, they'll usually divide into competing groups, and this tends to make people less happy. So he believes that schools which are small have a better chance of avoiding this problem.
All right. So what I'll do now is look at two schools here in New Zealand that are experimenting with a new approach.
So first, Russell School.

One interesting thing here is how the lessons are organized. Classrooms aren't set up like a lecture, you know, with the teacher in front talking to the group. Instead, everyone sits around a table similar to a meeting, and the teacher helps guide the students.
Then the teacher finds out what each individual student is interested in.

For example, one student was passionate about music, so the teacher asked him to record some music and then go about selling it to the public. In other words, establish his own business as part of classwork. And the students have been much more enthusiastic about school because of this practical approach.

Another idea at Russell School is to encourage students to plan for the future. They need to ask, "What do I want to do with my life? How will I achieve that?" And part of that process involves spending class time at the nearby university because this is a good way of getting them thinking about what comes after school.
Now, the other school I'll mention is South College.

Most children in this neighborhood come from families that aren't particularly wealthy, and the college is trying to respond to this. So, for example, the students each day when they first get to school, they get breakfast. It's a simple idea maybe, but it's increased the children's energy levels for the rest of the day.
Also at South College, parents have an important role. In class, they work alongside the teachers, and there's a good reason for this.
There's evidence that some children will acquire skills without a trained teacher, while for others, the teacher's role is more important.
Research has shown that this is particularly true of reading, so for some students, having a parent to supervise them in class is enough. Um,
then there's the classes themselves. How should students be grouped together?

Many people are surprised by the college's unusual approach to this. In the same class, the students aren't all necessarily the same age. They're sometimes different, and they seem to make just as much progress.
Okay, well, what conclusions can we draw?

A number of surveys have been done to try to answer this question, and one thing most students agree on is that at these schools, they've learned how to have more successful relationships with each other, with teachers, and with their own families. And that's obviously a significant finding.

And then there's another interesting idea that's come up. A study was done recently of past students at both schools. It found that these more positive attitudes didn't only help them at school. In fact, the same thing stayed with them later when they went into employment, and it's been a real asset.
So all of this has some bearing on the next question I'd like to ask you, which is-
That is the end of part four.
